newsitem.title: JAPAN: US commits $400 mln to world's poorest nations - ADB.
newsitem.headline: US commits $400 mln to world's poorest nations - ADB.

text.p: The United States has committed itself to contributing $400 million in loans to the world's poorest nations, despite pressure from some legislators in Washington to be less generous to multilateral agencies, Asian Development Bank (ADB) President Mitsuo Sato said on Friday.

The agreement was reached after a two-day meeting of ADB donors in Tokyo, where they negotiated the seventh replenishment of ADB's soft loan facility known as the Asian Development Fund (ADF), covering a four-year period to 2000.
But the amount was less than the pledge made by the United States in the sixth replenshiment, which stood at $680 million.
The United States has yet to fully honour that pledge, with $237 million still in arrears, but it has promised to pay that off in the next four years, Sato said.

"The significance of this is that it means we can maintain ADF as a single fund with full burden-sharing and participation by the United States during the entire replenishment period," Sato told a news conference.
Sato said his message to the U.S. Congress was that its contribution was of mutual benefit to the United States and Asian countries.

Donors such as the United States and European nations have been reluctant to commit new funding because of domestic budgetary constraints and because they feel that the newly wealthy Asian states should be shouldering more of the burden.
Asian donors agreed to increase their share of the burden in the concessionary fund in the latest agreement.
First-time contributors Malaysia and Thailand intend to provide $10 million and $4 million respectively.
South Korea, which has also graduated from borrower to lender, raised its contribution to $54.3 million compared with $15 million in the previous replenishment.
Singapore opted out from the seventh replenishment, but Sato said the ADB will continue to have talks with it on what it can do for the bank.
Japan remains the largest contributor with $1.02 billion.

Sato said he expected Hong Kong to boost its contribution in the concessionary fund from the previous replenishment. Although Taiwan and China are still contributing substantially, the amount would be slightly less than last time, he said.
Indonesia and the Philippines were also up for consideration to graduate from a borrower status, he said, adding that he thought it was possible for Indonesia to make a contribution to the scheme.
In effect, the contribution of the regional Asian donors would reach 50 percent of the total replenishment, Sato said.
North Korea has informally asked from time to time to be a member, but no formal approach has been made, he said.
The ADB donors agreed to contribute up to $3 billion in the seventh replenishment, compared to the previous $4.1 billion. ADB will provide the remaining $3.3 billion of the total $6.3 billion.
"In this climate of austerity, we are satisfied with the size of the ADF seven," Sato said.
Sato said Europe has maintained a strong commitment to the fund but their declined slightly than in the previous replenishment.

He said a condition made by many donors in the replenishment was that the bank review the graduation of borrower countries to donor status, the issue of loan "hardening" or making conditions stricter, and the ADB's financial policies, so that more funds could be channelled into the fund from the bank itself.
ADF loans, provided to the poorest of the ADB's developing member countries, are interest-free, have repayment periods of 30 years or more and carry a service charge of one percent annually.
